claim: Bach2 is a transcription repressor that actively participates in T and B lymphocyte development.
source: BTB domain And CNC Homolog 2 (Bach2) is a transcription repressor that actively participates in T and B lymphocyte development, but it is unknown if Bach2 is also involved in the development of innate immune cells, such as natural killer (NK) cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on Bach2 in T and B cells throughout the manuscript.

claim: Bach2 expression peaked in immature CD27+CD11b+ NK cells and decreased upon further maturation.
source: Here, we followed the expression of Bach2 during murine NK cell development, finding that it peaked in immature CD27+CD11b+ cells and decreased upon further maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D and western blot in Figure 1E.

claim: Bach2 showed an organ and tissue-specific expression pattern in NK cells.
source: Bach2 showed an organ and tissue-specific expression pattern in NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing Bach2 expression in NK cells from different tissues shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Bach2 expression positively correlated with the expression of transcription factor TCF1.
source: Bach2 expression positively correlated with the expression of transcription factor TCF1 and negatively correlated with genes encoding NK effector molecules and those involved in the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing downregulation of Tcf7 in Bach2-deficient NK cells (Figure 2B, 2C, 2E).

claim: Bach2 expression negatively correlated with genes encoding NK effector molecules and those involved in the cell cycle.
source: Bach2 expression positively correlated with the expression of transcription factor TCF1 and negatively correlated with genes encoding NK effector molecules and those involved in the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing upregulation of effector genes like Gzmb, Klrg1, and cell cycle genes in Bach2-deficient NK cells (Figure 2A, 2B).

claim: Lack of Bach2 expression caused changes in chromatin accessibility of corresponding genes.
source: Lack of Bach2 expression caused changes in chromatin accessibility of corresponding genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing differentially accessible regions in Bach2-deficient NK cells (Figure 3A).

claim: Bach2 deficiency resulted in increased proportions of terminally differentiated NK cells with increased production of granzymes and cytokines.
source: In the end, Bach2 deficiency resulted in increased proportions of terminally differentiated NK cells with increased production of granzymes and cytokines.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased CD27-CD11b+ NK cells and increased Granzyme B expression in Bach2cKO mice (Figures 2E, 2F, 4C).

claim: NK cell-mediated control of tumor metastasis was augmented in the absence of Bach2.
source: NK cell-mediated control of tumor metastasis was also augmented in the absence of Bach2.
evidence: This claim is supported by B16F10 tumor metastasis assay data showing reduced lung metastases in Bach2cKO mice (Figure 5A, 5B).

claim: Bach2 is a key checkpoint protein regulating NK terminal maturation.
source: Therefore, Bach2 is a key checkpoint protein regulating NK terminal maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including expression patterns, transcriptomics, chromatin accessibility, and functional data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Multipotent hematopoietic stem cells give rise to common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) that can differentiate into all types of lymphocytes.
source: Multipotent hematopoietic stem cells give rise to common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) that can differentiate into all types of lymphocytes.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of hematopoiesis.

claim: NK cell precursors (NKP) express IL-2R/IL-15R β chain (CD122), defining refined NK progenitors (rNKp).
source: NK cell precursors (NKP) are then derived and later express IL-2R/IL-15R β chain (CD122), defining refined NK progenitors (rNKp) (Carotta et al., 2011; Fathman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: At the rNKp stage in the mouse, commitment to NK cell development occurs, followed by the acquisition of the germline-encoded NK receptors NK1.1 and NKp46.
source: At this stage in the mouse, commitment to NK cell development occurs, followed by the acquisition of the germline-encoded NK receptors NK1.1 and NKp46, and the cells become immature NK cells.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of NK cell development.

claim: Mature NK cells develop when they gain the expression of DX5 (CD49b), cytotoxic activity, and capacity to produce interferon-γ (IFNγ).
source: Mature NK cells develop when they gain the expression of DX5 (CD49b), cytotoxic activity, and capacity to produce interferon-γ (IFNγ) (Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Mature NK cells can be further defined based upon the differential expression of CD27 and CD11b, progressing from CD27+CD11b- to CD27+CD11b+ to CD27-CD11b+ cells.
source: Mature NK cells can be further defined based upon the differential expression of CD27 and CD11b. Starting from double-negative cells being the most immature cells regarding their functionality, the cells upregulate the expression of CD27 then CD11b to become CD27+CD11b- (CD27+ cells) then CD27+CD11b+ (double-positive) respectively, which undergo homeostatic expansion. Finally, the double-positive cells lose the expression of CD27 and retain expression of CD11b to become terminally differentiated NK cells (CD11b+ cells) with increased cytotoxic activity (Chiossone et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: CD27-CD11b+ NK cells are terminally differentiated with increased cytotoxic activity.
source: Finally, the double-positive cells lose the expression of CD27 and retain expression of CD11b to become terminally differentiated NK cells (CD11b+ cells) with increased cytotoxic activity (Chiossone et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Eomesodermin has been identified as a unique factor required for NK development, distinct from ILC1s.
source: Eomesodermin has been identified as a unique factor required for NK development, distinct from ILC1s which share many similarities in surface makers with NK cells (Gordon et al., 2012; Intlekofer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Kruppel-like factor 2 intrinsically regulates NK cell homeostasis by limiting early-stage NK cell proliferation and guiding them toward trans-presented IL-15.
source: Kruppel-like factor 2 intrinsically regulates NK cell homeostasis by limiting early-stage NK cell proliferation and guiding them toward trans-presented IL-15 (Rabacal et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: IRF8 is required for the effector functions of NK cells against viral infection.
source: IRF8 is required for the effector functions of NK cells against viral infection (Adams et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: T-bet positively regulates the terminal maturation of NK cells.
source: T-bet has a broader function in various cells including T cells, ILC1s, and NK cells, and positively regulates the terminal maturation of NK cells (Townsend et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Zeb2 promotes NK terminal differentiation and may function downstream of T-bet.
source: Similarly, Zeb2 promotes NK terminal differentiation and may function downstream of T-bet (van Helden et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Blimp-1 is expressed throughout NK cell maturation and is required for NK homeostasis.
source: Blimp-1 is expressed throughout NK cell maturation and is required for NK homeostasis (Kallies et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: TCF1 participates in the development of NK cells and its downregulation is required for NK terminal maturation.
source: TCF1 (encoded by Tcf7) participates in the development of NK cells and its downregulation is required for NK terminal maturation (Jeevan-Raj et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: High expression of TCF1 correlated with genes expressed in immature NK cells including Cd27, Xcl1, and Kit.
source: A multi-tissue single-cell analysis divided NK cells into two major groups based on TCF1 levels: high expression of TCF1 correlated with genes expressed in immature NK cells including Cd27, Xcl1, and Kit while TCF1 was inversely correlated with the expression of genes involved in effector function such as Gzmb, Gzma, Ccl5, and Klrg1 (McFarland et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: TCF1 was inversely correlated with the expression of genes involved in effector function such as Gzmb, Gzma, Ccl5, and Klrg1.
source: A multi-tissue single-cell analysis divided NK cells into two major groups based on TCF1 levels: high expression of TCF1 correlated with genes expressed in immature NK cells including Cd27, Xcl1, and Kit while TCF1 was inversely correlated with the expression of genes involved in effector function such as Gzmb, Gzma, Ccl5, and Klrg1 (McFarland et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bach2 was identified as a transcriptional repressor that forms a heterodimer with Maf family proteins and binds to T-MARE (TGCTGA G/C TCAGCA).
source: The transcription factor, BTB domain And CNC Homolog 2 (Bach2), was identified as a transcriptional repressor. It forms a heterodimer with Maf family proteins and binds to a DNA motif called T-MARE (TGCTGA G/C TCAGCA), a Maf recognition element (MARE), to regulate gene expression (Muto et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The regulatory function of Bach2 is mediated through its interaction with the super-enhancers (SEs).
source: The regulatory function of Bach2 is mediated through its interaction with the super-enhancers (SEs), and its aberrant expression is associated with a variety of autoimmune diseases as well as cancers (Afzali et al., 2017; Marroquí et al., 2014; Roychoudhuri et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Aberrant expression of Bach2 is associated with a variety of autoimmune diseases as well as cancers.
source: The regulatory function of Bach2 is mediated through its interaction with the super-enhancers (SEs), and its aberrant expression is associated with a variety of autoimmune diseases as well as cancers (Afzali et al., 2017; Marroquí et al., 2014; Roychoudhuri et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bach2 is expressed in CLP and represses genes of myeloid lineage to promote the development of cells in the lymphoid lineage.
source: Bach2 is expressed in CLP and represses genes of myeloid lineage to promote the development of cells in the lymphoid lineage (Itoh-Nakadai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bach2 was first shown to be a B cell-intrinsic transcription factor that regulates B cell development through inhibiting the expression of Blimp-1 (encoded by Prdm1).
source: Bach2 was first shown to be a B cell-intrinsic transcription factor that regulates B cell development through inhibiting the expression of Blimp-1 (encoded by Prdm1) (Muto et al., 1998; Ochiai et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The rapid upregulation of Blimp-1 mediated by Bach2 deficiency promotes the terminal differentiation of B cells toward plasma cells even prior to class-switch recombination (CSR).
source: The rapid upregulation of Blimp-1 mediated by Bach2 deficiency promotes the terminal differentiation of B cells toward plasma cells even prior to class-switch recombination (CSR) (Muto et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions, Bach2 maintains T cells in a naïve state, preventing the generation of effector T cells by inhibiting the expression of effector molecules downstream of TCR signaling.
source: Under homeostatic conditions, Bach2 maintains T cells in a naïve state, preventing the generation of effector T cells by inhibiting the expression of effector molecules downstream of TCR signaling (Roychoudhuri et al., 2016a; Tsukumo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bach2 expression is reduced during T cell polarization.
source: Bach2 expression is reduced during T cell polarization while higher expression of Bach2 in CD4+ T cell differentiation promotes the formation of regulatory T cells by repressing genes related to effector differentiation within helper T cell lineages (Lahmann et al., 2019; Roychoudhuri et al., 2016a; Roychoudhuri et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Higher expression of Bach2 in CD4+ T cell differentiation promotes the formation of regulatory T cells by repressing genes related to effector differentiation within helper T cell lineages.
source: Bach2 expression is reduced during T cell polarization while higher expression of Bach2 in CD4+ T cell differentiation promotes the formation of regulatory T cells by repressing genes related to effector differentiation within helper T cell lineages (Lahmann et al., 2019; Roychoudhuri et al., 2016a; Roychoudhuri et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Regaining the expression of Bach2 after differentiation downregulated pro-inflammatory signals and differentiation into T cell memory cell lineages.
source: Regaining the expression of Bach2 after differentiation downregulated pro-inflammatory signals and differentiation into T cell memory cell lineages (Herndler-Brandstetter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bach2 expression was detected in CLPs and expression was relatively reduced in pre-NK progenitor cells and rNKp.
source: Bach2 expression was detected in CLPs and expression was relatively reduced in pre-NK progenitor cells and rNKp (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), reflecting the critical role of Bach2 in the development of lymphoid cells from CLPs (Itoh-Nakadai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bach2 was homogenously expressed by NK cells in both the BM and spleen at the rNKp stage.
source: Bach2 was homogenously expressed by these NK cells in both the BM and spleen (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mature NK cells had higher Bach2 expression than immature NK cells in both the BM and spleen.
source: In both the BM and spleen, Bach2 expression was detected in both immature (DX5–NK1.1+) and mature (DX5+NK1.1+) NK cells while mature NK cells had even higher Bach2 expression than the immature NK cells (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The expression of Bach2 was lowest in the most mature CD27-CD11b+ cells compared with the other two stages.
source: Surprisingly, the expression of Bach2 was lowest in the most mature CD27-CD11b+ cells compared with the other two stages (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and western blot in Figure 1E.

claim: At the bulk splenic NK cell population level, the expression of Bach2 inversely correlated with the age of the mice.
source: At the bulk splenic NK cell population level, the expression of Bach2 inversely correlated with the age of the mice: 2-week-old mice had the highest expression, and 12-week-old mice had the lowest expression of Bach2 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: More than 60% of NK cells were immature CD27+CD11b- cells with less than 3% of mature CD27-CD11b+ cells in 2-week-old mice.
source: More than 60% of NK cells were immature CD27+CD11b- cells with less than 3% of mature CD27-CD11b+ cells in 2-week-old mice while around 40% of NK cells in 12-week-old mice were in the most mature CD27-CD11b+ stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Around 40% of NK cells in 12-week-old mice were in the most mature CD27-CD11b+ stage.
source: More than 60% of NK cells were immature CD27+CD11b- cells with less than 3% of mature CD27-CD11b+ cells in 2-week-old mice while around 40% of NK cells in 12-week-old mice were in the most mature CD27-CD11b+ stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 2-week-old NK cells showed higher Bach2 levels than their 12-week-old counterparts in each corresponding NK subset.
source: Moreover, 2-week-old NK cells showed higher Bach2 levels than their 12-week-old counterparts in each corresponding NK subset (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Bach2 expression was detected in NK cells in various different tissues, such as lymph nodes, lung, and liver.
source: The effect of Bach2 on NK cells may not be restricted to splenic NK cells; we also detected Bach2 expression in NK cells in various different tissues, such as lymph nodes, lung, and liver (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Bach2 showed similar expression levels in lymph node and liver as compared to spleen while in the lung, the expression was much lower.
source: Bach2 showed similar expression levels in lymph node and liver as compared to spleen while in the lung, the expression was much lower.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Exons 1–2, including the start codon, had been deleted in essentially all Bach2cKO NK cells.
source: Examination of Bach2 mRNA showed that exons 1–2, including the start codon, had been deleted in essentially all Bach2cKO NK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), confirming deletion of Bach2 expression in Bach2cKO NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD94 showed significant downregulation in Bach2-deficient NK cells.
source: When we assessed the expression of NK cell inhibitory and activation receptors (Ly49s and NKG2A/CD94), we did not find any changes in the expressed repertoire of these receptors with Bach2 deficiency except CD94 showed significant downregulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Genetic deletion of CD94 in NK cells did not affect the development and function of NK cells.
source: However, it was previously reported that genetic deletion of CD94 in NK cells did not affect the development and function of NK cells (Orr et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: 133 genes were downregulated and 210 genes were upregulated in Bach2cKO NK cells as compared to control NK cells.
source: Overall, we found 133 genes downregulated and 210 genes upregulated in Bach2cKO NK cells as compared to control NK cells (Bach2cKO versus control) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The transcripts with decreased expression in Bach2cKO NK cells corresponded to genes involved in T cell differentiation, cell development, and cell homeostasis pathways.
source: The transcripts with decreased expression corresponded to genes involved in T cell differentiation, cell development, and cell homeostasis pathways (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The top 2 downregulated genes in Bach2cKO NK cells were Kit and Tcf7.
source: Specifically, the top 2 downregulated genes were Kit and Tcf7 (Figure 2B), which were previously shown to be responsible in maintaining the stemness of the T cells (Siddiqui et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Kit and Tcf7 were previously shown to be responsible in maintaining the stemness of T cells.
source: Specifically, the top 2 downregulated genes were Kit and Tcf7 (Figure 2B), which were previously shown to be responsible in maintaining the stemness of the T cells (Siddiqui et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The loss of Tcf7 expression led to enhanced NK cell terminal maturation.
source: Regarding NK cells, the loss of Tcf7 expression led to enhanced NK cell terminal maturation (Jeevan-Raj et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Cd27, Ccr7, and Cd69 were downregulated in Bach2cKO NK cells.
source: We also detected the downregulation of Cd27, Ccr7, and Cd69 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The downregulation of Ccr7 was previously shown to be correlated with human NK cell differentiation toward effector phenotype.
source: The downregulation of Ccr7 was previously shown to be correlated with human NK cell differentiation toward effector phenotype (Hong et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The transcripts with elevated expression in Bach2cKO NK cells included genes involved in the cell cycle, cell proliferation, and inflammatory response pathways.
source: On the other hand, the transcripts with elevated expression included genes involved in the cell cycle, cell proliferation, and inflammatory response pathways (Figure 2A), suggesting a skewing toward an effector phenotype as a result of Bach2 deficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Among the upregulated genes in Bach2cKO NK cells were those associated with NK cell effector functions such as Klrg1, Gzmb, Gzmk, and Ccl5.
source: Indeed, among the upregulated genes were those associated with NK cell effector functions such as Klrg1, Gzmb, Gzmk, and Ccl5 (Figure 2B; Bezman et al., 2012), indicating that lack of Bach2 expression facilitated the differentiation of NK cells toward terminal maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B and citation to prior research.

claim: Tcf7, Kit, and Sox6 showed significantly lower expression in Bach2-deficient NK cells by qPCR analysis.
source: We detected significantly lower expression of genes, for example, Tcf7, Kit, and Sox6 in Bach2-deficient NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cd39, Klrg1, Gzmb, Klrb1b, and Ccl5 were increased in Bach2-deficient NK cells by qPCR analysis.
source: Regarding genes upregulated in the RNA-seq analysis, we confirmed Cd39, Klrg1, Gzmb, Klrb1b, and Ccl5 to be increased by qPCR analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Kit, CD69, and TCF1 were significantly downregulated in Bach2-deficient NK cells at the protein level.
source: Consistent with their transcription level, the proteins encoded by these genes were changed accordingly with Bach2 deficiency. Kit, CD69, and TCF1 (encoded by Tcf7) were significantly downregulated in Bach2-deficient NK cells while CD62L (encoded by Sell) did not show difference at the protein level (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: CD62L did not show difference at the protein level between Bach2-deficient and control NK cells.
source: Kit, CD69, and TCF1 (encoded by Tcf7) were significantly downregulated in Bach2-deficient NK cells while CD62L (encoded by Sell) did not show difference at the protein level (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: CD39, KLRG1, CX3CR1, and Granzyme B were elevated in Bach2-deficient NK cells at the protein level.
source: On the other hand, CD39, KLRG1, CX3CR1, and Granzyme B were elevated, consistent with their changes at the RNA level (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: No difference in Ki67 expression was found between Bach2cKO and control NK cells.
source: Although we detected increased expression of multiple genes involved in cell cycle and proliferation, we did not find a difference in Ki67 expression between Bach2cKO and control NK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Enforced Bach2 expression in exhausted CD8+ T cells resulted in the cells becoming exclusively stem-like precursor, exhausted CD8+ T cells, preventing their further differentiation into terminal exhausted CD8+ T cells.
source: It was reported that the enforced Bach2 expression in exhausted CD8+ T cells resulted in the cells becoming exclusively stem-like precursor, exhausted CD8+ T cells, preventing their further differentiation into terminal exhausted CD8+ T cells (Yao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Genes upregulated in NK cells induced by Bach2 deficiency positively correlated with terminal differentiated effector-like gene signatures.
source: We found genes upregulated in NK cells induced by Bach2 deficiency positively correlated with terminal differentiated effector-like gene signatures (Figure 2G) whereas the genes downregulated showed a stem-like signature (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Genes downregulated in NK cells induced by Bach2 deficiency showed a stem-like signature.
source: We found genes upregulated in NK cells induced by Bach2 deficiency positively correlated with terminal differentiated effector-like gene signatures (Figure 2G) whereas the genes downregulated showed a stem-like signature (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Bach2-sufficient NK cells displayed a naïve CD8+ T cell signature.
source: We found that Bach2-sufficient NK cells displayed a naïve CD8+ T cell signature (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) while Bach2-deficient NK cells resembled activated effector CD8+ T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Bach2-deficient NK cells resembled activated effector CD8+ T cells.
source: We found that Bach2-sufficient NK cells displayed a naïve CD8+ T cell signature (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) while Bach2-deficient NK cells resembled activated effector CD8+ T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: 564 regions were found to be upregulated and 251 were found to be downregulated in Bach2-deficient NK cells as compared to Bach2-sufficient NK cells by ATAC-seq.
source: Within the differentially accessible regions (DARs) identified by ATAC-seq, 564 regions were found to be upregulated and 251 were found to be downregulated in Bach2-deficient NK cells as compared to Bach2-sufficient NK cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: With Bach2 deficiency, the DARs indicated overall increased chromatin accessibility in the genome.
source: Thus, with Bach2 deficiency, the DARs indicated overall increased chromatin accessibility in the genome, consistent with the putative function of Bach2 as a repressor in NK cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ATAC-seq data showing more upregulated than downregulated regions.

claim: The upregulated DARs contained motifs bound by the transcription factors IRF8, Bach1, Bach2, and AP-1.
source: The upregulated DARs contained motifs bound by the transcription factors IRF8, Bach1, Bach2, and AP-1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: IRF8-mediated signaling is required for NK cell maturation and function.
source: Prior studies indicated IRF8-mediated signaling is required for NK cell maturation and function (Mace et al., 2017), suggesting increased accessibility of IRF8-regulated genes in Bach2 deficiency thus may result in bias toward NK cell development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The enriched binding motifs by Bach1, Bach2, Fra2, and AP-1 in upregulated DARs all contained a common binding sequence (5'-TGA(C/G)TCA-3').
source: Interestingly, we found that the enriched binding motifs by Bach1, Bach2, Fra2 (Fos-related Antigen 2, an AP-1 transcription factor subunit), and AP-1 in upregulated DARs all contained a common binding sequence (5'-TGA(C/G)TCA-3') (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In CD8+ T cells, Bach2 has been reported to share this common binding sequence with the AP-1 transcription factor family and compete with AP-1 factors for the access to the target genes.
source: In CD8+ T cells, Bach2 has been reported to share this common binding sequence with the AP-1 transcription factor family and compete with AP-1 factors for the access to the target genes due to the similarity in their binding motifs (Roychoudhuri et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The direct target genes of Bach2 in CD8+ T cells, such as Irf8, Ccl3, Ccl4, and Gzmb, showed elevated expression in Bach2cKO NK cells.
source: Indeed, we found the direct target genes of Bach2 in CD8+ T cells, such as Irf8, Ccl3, Ccl4, and Gzmb, showed elevated expression in Bach2cKO NK cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was increased JunD occupancy in the absence of Bach2 in NK cells.
source: Also, there was increased JunD occupancy in the absence of Bach2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) in NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The motifs enriched in downregulated DARs were mostly TCF/LEF family protein-binding motifs.
source: The motifs enriched in downregulated DARs were mostly TCF/LEF family protein-binding motifs (Figure 3B), especially the binding motif for TCF1 (encoded by Tcf7) that was also one of the top downregulated genes in Bach2cKO NK cells (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Deficiency of Tcf7 and its downstream genes promoted the terminal differentiation of NK cells as well as CD8+ T cells.
source: Deficiency of Tcf7 and its downstream genes promoted the terminal differentiation of NK cells as well as CD8+ T cells (Jeevan-Raj et al., 2017; Utzschneider et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Blimp-1 has been widely studied as a direct target of Bach2 in B cell and T cells.
source: For example, Blimp-1 has been widely studied as a direct target of Bach2 in B cell and T cells (Kometani et al., 2013; Muto et al., 2004; Ochiai et al., 2006; Roychoudhuri et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Both Prdm1 and Irf8 genes displayed increased accessibility with Bach2 deficiency.
source: By ATAC-seq we found that both Prdm1 and Irf8 genes displayed increased accessibility with Bach2 deficiency (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There were Bach2-binding motifs in the DARs of Prdm1 and Irf8, suggesting a direct regulatory function of Bach2 on these genes.
source: Furthermore, there were Bach2-binding motifs in the DARs, suggesting a direct regulatory function of Bach2 on Prdm1 and Irf8 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data and motif analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Prdm1 and Irf8 were shown to be upregulated at RNA level by both RNA-seq and qPCR in Bach2-deficient NK cells.
source: In Bach2-deficient NK cells, Prdm1 and Irf8 were shown to be upregulated at RNA level by both RNA-seq and qPCR (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At the protein level, Blimp-1 did not show corresponding changes between NK cells from Bach2cKO and control mice.
source: However, at the protein level, we failed to detect the corresponding changes of Blimp-1 compared between NK cells from Bach2cKO and control mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: IRF8 was significantly upregulated in Bach2-deficient NK cells at the protein level.
source: Surprisingly, we found that IRF8 was significantly upregulated in Bach2-deficient NK cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The loss of IRF8 resulted in impaired terminal maturation of NK cells.
source: Given that the loss of IRF8 resulted in impaired terminal maturation of NK cells (Mace et al., 2017), Bach2 may repress the expression of IRF8 directly or indirectly to affect NK cell development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the BM, no significant difference was observed between control and Bach2cKO mice regarding the frequency of the CD27+ cells or CD11b+ cells.
source: In the BM, we did not observe any significant difference between control and Bach2cKO mice regarding the frequency of the CD27+ cells or CD11b+ cells (Figure 4A) although total NK cell numbers were reduced in Bach2cKO mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Total NK cell numbers were reduced in Bach2cKO mice in the BM.
source: In the BM, we did not observe any significant difference between control and Bach2cKO mice regarding the frequency of the CD27+ cells or CD11b+ cells (Figure 4A) although total NK cell numbers were reduced in Bach2cKO mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: An altered maturation profile of NK cells was detected in the spleen of Bach2cKO mice with more cells having the mature NK cell phenotype (CD11b+) and fewer cells at the immature DP stage.
source: We detected an altered maturation profile of NK cells in the spleen of Bach2cKO mice with more cells having the mature NK cell phenotype (CD11b+) and fewer cells at the immature DP stage as compared to control mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The total number of NK cells was unchanged in the spleen of Bach2cKO mice.
source: However, the total number of NK cells was unchanged in the spleen (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The expression of KLRG1 was increased at the population level in Bach2cKO NK cells.
source: As we previously showed, the expression of KLRG1, a marker of terminally mature splenic NK cells was also increased at the population level (Figure 2E), further confirming biased development into terminally mature NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The frequency of CD27+CD11b+ NK cells was significantly reduced while the frequency of CD27-CD11b+ NK cells was markedly increased in both BM and spleen in Bach2-/- mice.
source: Similar to the results presented in Bach2cKO mice, we found the frequency of CD27+CD11b+ NK cells was significantly reduced while the frequency of CD27-CD11b+ NK cells was markedly increased in both BM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and spleen (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) in Bach2-/- mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: The expression of KLRG1 was upregulated and more cells (~80%) expressed KLRG1 in Bach2-/- mice compared to Bach2-sufficient mice (~50%).
source: In agreement, the expression of KLRG1 was upregulated and we also found more cells (~80%) expressing KLRG1 in Bach2-/- mice compared to Bach2-sufficient mice (~50%) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No significant changes in NK cell maturation were found in lymph nodes of Bach2cKO mice.
source: We did not find significant changes in NK cell maturation in lymph nodes (Figure 4E) whereas a reduced NK cell number was found (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A reduced NK cell number was found in lymph nodes of Bach2cKO mice.
source: We did not find significant changes in NK cell maturation in lymph nodes (Figure 4E) whereas a reduced NK cell number was found (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In liver, increased terminal maturation of NK cells was observed in Bach2cKO mice.
source: In liver, we observed a similar pattern as we found in spleen, with increased terminal maturation of NK cells (Figure 4G) but we failed to see changes in NK cell number (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: No changes in NK cell number were found in liver of Bach2cKO mice.
source: In liver, we observed a similar pattern as we found in spleen, with increased terminal maturation of NK cells (Figure 4G) but we failed to see changes in NK cell number (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Lung displayed a unique profile of NK maturation with most of the NK cells falling into the most mature NK subset in control mice.
source: Interestingly, lung displayed a unique profile of NK maturation with most of the NK cells falling into the most mature NK subset in control mice (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: An increased percentage of CD27-CD11b+ cells was detected in lung with Bach2 deficiency.
source: Even while biased toward this subset, we still detected an increased percentage of CD27-CD11b+ cells with Bach2 deficiency (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: More NK cells were detected in lung from Bach2cKO mice.
source: Different from other tissues, we also detected more NK cells in lung from Bach2cKO mice (Figure 4J), suggesting a preferential homing of terminally matured NK cells into the lung.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The lung metastases of B16F10 tumors in Bach2cKO mice were dramatically reduced compared to control mice.
source: The lung metastases of B16F10 tumors in Bach2cKO mice were dramatically reduced compared to control mice (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor metastasis assay data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The control of tumor metastases was NK cell-dependent because both Bach2cKO mice and control mice displayed a similar number of metastatic tumor colonies when NK cells were depleted with anti-NK1.1 (PK136).
source: This control of tumor metastases was NK cell-dependent because both Bach2cKO mice and control mice displayed a similar number of metastatic tumor colonies when NK cells were depleted with anti-NK1.1 (PK136) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor metastasis assay data with NK cell depletion shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: No difference in killing B16F10 cells was seen between Bach2cKO and control NK cells in vitro.
source: However, we did not see any difference in killing B16F10 cells between Bach2cKO and control NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No difference in IFNγ production was detected in response to various stimulations between Bach2cKO and control splenic NK cells.
source: We also assessed IFNγ production in response to various stimulations including anti-NK1.1, IL-15, and IL-12 plus IL-18 on splenic NK cells. We did not detect any difference with or without Bach2 expression in NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lung NK cells displayed similar levels of Granzyme B expression between control and Bach2cKO mice at steady state.
source: Although splenic NK cells lacking Bach2 showed increased Granzyme B expression, lung NK cells displayed similar levels of Granzyme B expression between control and Bach2cKO mice at steady state (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NK cells effectively cleared disseminated tumor cells from the lung within 24 hr of tumor inoculation.
source: Since it had been shown that NK cells effectively cleared disseminated tumor cells from the lung within 24 hr of tumor inoculation (Ichise et al., 2022), we tested the NK function in vivo in the lung 24 hr after tumor injection in Bach2cKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Increased NK cells were observed in the lung in Bach2cKO mice 24 hr after tumor injection.
source: We observed increased NK cells in the lung in Bach2cKO mice (Figure 5C) similar to the phenotype at steady state (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No more proliferating NK cells were detected in the lungs in Bach2cKO mice after tumor injection.
source: We did not detect more proliferating NK cells in the lungs in Bach2cKO mice after tumor injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that NK cell migration may cause the increased lung NK cell numbers in Bach2cKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: NK cells displayed a biased maturation profile toward CD27-CD11b+ NK cells in Bach2cKO mice compared to control mice after tumor challenge.
source: NK cells also displayed a biased maturation profile toward CD27-CD11b+ NK cells (Figure 5D) as well as increased proportion of KLRG1+ cells (Figure 5E) in Bach2cKO mice compared to control mice after tumor challenge.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Increased proportion of KLRG1+ cells was observed in Bach2cKO mice compared to control mice after tumor challenge.
source: NK cells also displayed a biased maturation profile toward CD27-CD11b+ NK cells (Figure 5D) as well as increased proportion of KLRG1+ cells (Figure 5E) in Bach2cKO mice compared to control mice after tumor challenge.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The terminally developed CD27lowKLRG1+CD11bhigh NK subsets are crucial in clearing the early metastatic colorectal carcinoma in mice.
source: Studies have shown that the terminally developed CD27lowKLRG1+CD11bhigh NK subsets are crucial in clearing the early metastatic colorectal carcinoma in mice (Malaisé et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bach2 is highly expressed in functional immature NK cells (CD27+ cells) and gradually downregulates its expression at the terminal stage of NK maturation (CD11b+ cells).
source: Here, we found that Bach2 is highly expressed in functional immature NK cells (CD27+ cells) and gradually downregulates its expression at the terminal stage of NK maturation (CD11b+ cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and western blot data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Bach2 deficiency caused a biased NK cell development toward terminal differentiation in an NK cell-intrinsic manner.
source: In line with this, we demonstrated that Bach2 deficiency caused a biased NK cell development toward terminal differentiation in an NK cell-intrinsic manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing NK cell maturation profiles in Bach2cKO and control mice (Figure 4).

claim: Bach2-deficient NK cells displayed increased cytotoxic gene expression and chromatin accessibility.
source: Bach2-deficient NK cells also displayed increased cytotoxic gene expression and chromatin accessibility and were more potent in controlling tumor metastases.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2) and ATAC-seq data (Figure 3).

claim: Bach2-deficient NK cells were more potent in controlling tumor metastases.
source: Bach2-deficient NK cells also displayed increased cytotoxic gene expression and chromatin accessibility and were more potent in controlling tumor metastases.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor metastasis assay data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Bach2 plays a critical role in the development of lymphoid cells by repressing the expression of genes important for myeloid cells in CLP.
source: Bach2 plays a critical role in the development of lymphoid cells: its presence in CLP repressed the expression of genes important for myeloid cells, promoting the development of T and B cells (Itoh-Nakadai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the BM, the expression of Bach2 increased after commitment of stem cells to the B cell lineage with its expression high in pre-pro B cells, pro-B cells, pre-B cells, and immature B cells.
source: However, in the BM, the expression of Bach2 increased after commitment of stem cells to the B cell lineage with its expression high in pre-pro B cells, pro-B cells, pre-B cells, and immature B cells.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of Bach2 expression in B cell development.

claim: Bach2 served as a checkpoint protein in B cells that inhibited the expression of the immunoglobulin heavy chain of activated p53 by competing with BCL6 for functional VDJ rearrangements.
source: Bach2 served as a checkpoint protein in B cells that inhibited the expression of the immunoglobulin heavy chain of activated p53 by competing with BCL6 for functional VDJ rearrangements (Muto et al., 1998; Swaminathan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bach2 suppressed the differentiation of activated B cells to plasma cells by inhibiting the expression of Blimp-1, which allowed CSR and somatic hypermutation to take place before becoming plasma cells.
source: Bach2 also suppressed the differentiation of activated B cells to plasma cells by inhibiting the expression of Blimp-1 (encoded by Prdm1 gene), which allowed CSR and somatic hypermutation to take place before becoming plasma cells (Kometani et al., 2013; Muto et al., 2004; Ochiai et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bach2 started to gain its expression in NK cells after the acquisition of germline-encoded NK receptors such as NK1.1 and NKp46.
source: We showed that Bach2 started to gain its expression in NK cells after the acquisition of germline-encoded NK receptors such as NK1.1 and NKp46, a stage when NK cells displayed an effector program.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Maturing NK cells upregulate CD27 transiently followed by the upregulation of CD11b and KLRG1.
source: Interestingly, maturing NK cells upregulate CD27 transiently followed by the upregulation of CD11b and KLRG1 (Chiossone et al., 2009; Huntington et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During the transition from CD27+ to CD11b+ NK cells, NK cells lose their homeostatic expansion capacity but acquire cytotoxic activity.
source: During this transition, NK cells lose their homeostatic expansion capacity but acquire cytotoxic activity (Chiossone et al., 2009; Huntington et al., 2007), suggesting the main role of Bach2 is to suppress the functional development of the most mature NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tcf7 is highly expressed in naïve T cells, decreased in effector T cells, and regained its expression in memory cells, showing its role in maintaining pluripotency of the T cells.
source: Tcf7 (encoding TCF1) is highly expressed in naïve T cells, decreased in effector T cells, and regained its expression in memory cells, showing its role in maintaining pluripotency of the T cells (Willinger et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TCF1 was recently shown to be a hallmark of stem-like precursor exhausted CD8+ T cells with self-renewal capability and can differentiate into terminal effector-like exhausted CD8+ T cells which lacked TCF1 expression.
source: On the other hand, TCF1 was recently shown to be a hallmark of stem-like precursor exhausted CD8+ T cells with self-renewal capability and can differentiate into terminal effector-like exhausted CD8+ T cells which lacked TCF1 expression (Utzschneider et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bach2 played a positive role in maintaining the pool of stem-like precursors exhausted CD8+ T cells as enforced overexpression of Bach2 resulted in the cells retaining this stem-like condition while knockout of Bach2 led to terminal differentiation of the cells.
source: It was shown that Bach2 also played a positive role in maintaining the pool of these stem-like precursors exhausted CD8+ T cells as enforced overexpression of Bach2 resulted in the cells retaining this stem-like condition while knockout of Bach2 led to terminal differentiation of the cells (Yao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bach2 deficiency caused downregulation of TCF1 transcription in NK cells.
source: Our data in NK cells also showed the link between Bach2 and TCF1 as Bach2 deficiency caused downregulation of TCF1 transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Bach2 may antagonize RUNX3 to induce TCF1 expression in CD8+ T cells.
source: Unlike CD8+ T cells in which Bach2 may antagonize RUNX3 to induce TCF1 expression (Yao et al., 2021), we did not detect changes in RUNX3 expression in NK cells, indicating a different regulatory circuit between Bach2 and TCF1 in NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: No changes in RUNX3 expression were detected in Bach2-deficient NK cells.
source: Unlike CD8+ T cells in which Bach2 may antagonize RUNX3 to induce TCF1 expression (Yao et al., 2021), we did not detect changes in RUNX3 expression in NK cells, indicating a different regulatory circuit between Bach2 and TCF1 in NK cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statement that a different regulatory circuit exists in NK cells.

claim: BCL6 was downregulated in Bach2cKO NK cells.
source: We found that BCL6 was downregulated in Bach2cKO NK cells while BCL6 was recently reported to directly bind the regulatory region of Tcf7 and promoted its expression in memory CD8+ T cells (Liu et al., 2019), indicating that Bach2 can induce BCL6 expression (a similar positive correlation was found in B cells) (Huang et al., 2014) and promote TCF1 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: BCL6 was recently reported to directly bind the regulatory region of Tcf7 and promoted its expression in memory CD8+ T cells.
source: We found that BCL6 was downregulated in Bach2cKO NK cells while BCL6 was recently reported to directly bind the regulatory region of Tcf7 and promoted its expression in memory CD8+ T cells (Liu et al., 2019), indicating that Bach2 can induce BCL6 expression (a similar positive correlation was found in B cells) (Huang et al., 2014) and promote TCF1 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bach2 can induce BCL6 expression in B cells.
source: We found that BCL6 was downregulated in Bach2cKO NK cells while BCL6 was recently reported to directly bind the regulatory region of Tcf7 and promoted its expression in memory CD8+ T cells (Liu et al., 2019), indicating that Bach2 can induce BCL6 expression (a similar positive correlation was found in B cells) (Huang et al., 2014) and promote TCF1 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Only a minor decrease of TCF1 at the protein level was detected in Bach2-deficient NK cells.
source: Thus, the pathways for Bach2 to regulate TCF1 may incorporate pathways shared by both B cells and T cells but since we only detected a minor decrease of TCF1 at the protein level in Bach2-deficient NK cells, to what extent Bach2-TCF1 regulation impacts NK development requires further investigation.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: Blimp-1 was uncovered to be the target of Bach2 in both B cells and T cells to regulate cell differentiation and function.
source: Regarding how Bach2 functions in NK cells as compared to other lymphoid cells, Blimp-1 was uncovered to be the target of Bach2 in both B cells and T cells to regulate cell differentiation and function (Ochiai et al., 2006; Roychoudhuri et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Regulome analysis of human NK cells proposed that Bach2-mediated gene suppression relied upon inhibiting Blimp-1 expression, and Blimp-1 repressed the TCF1-LEF1-MYC-induced homeostatic expansion of NK cells.
source: Regulome analysis of human NK cells also proposed that Bach2-mediated gene suppression relied upon inhibiting Blimp-1 expression, and Blimp-1 repressed the TCF1-LEF1-MYC-induced homeostatic expansion of NK cells (Collins et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Prdm1 is not the major target of Bach2 in regulating NK cell differentiation.
source: However, in our data, we did not detect changes in Blimp-1 protein expression except for a slight upregulation at the mRNA level in Bach2-deficient NK cells, indicating Prdm1 is not the major target of Bach2 in regulating NK cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of protein-level changes despite mRNA changes.

claim: Bach2 may repress IRF8 transcription directly since Bach2-binding motifs were found within the intron region of Irf8.
source: Bach2 may repress IRF8 transcription directly since we found Bach2-binding motifs within the intron region.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data and motif analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There are three MafK-binding sites within the Irf8 locus.
source: A recent study shows that there are three MafK-binding sites within the Irf8 locus (Fourier et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bach2 has been shown to act together with MafK to bind to the MAREs and negatively regulate B cell function.
source: As Bach2 has been shown to act together with MafK to bind to the MAREs and negatively regulate B cell function (Muto et al., 1998), it is possible that a similar mechanism may occur in NK cell regulation by Bach2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The mammalian target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) inhibits FoxO1 to reduce Bach2 mRNA expression in B cells.
source: Studies in B cells showed that the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) inhibits FoxO1 to reduce Bach2 mRNA expression (Tamahara et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: FoxO1 was found to directly bind within and proximal to the Bach2 gene locus in CD8 T cells.
source: Interestingly, FoxO1 was found to directly bind within and proximal to the Bach2 gene locus in CD8 T cells (Delpoux et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Upon T cell activation, FoxO1 induces the Bach2 transcripts to compete with AP-1 factors for AP-1-binding sites.
source: Upon T cell activation, FoxO1 induces the Bach2 transcripts to compete with AP-1 factors for AP-1-binding sites (Delpoux et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In NK cells, FoxO1 suppresses NK cell maturation by repressing T-bet.
source: In NK cells, FoxO1 suppresses NK cell maturation by repressing T-bet (Deng et al., 2015) and mTORC2 was also found to regulate T-bet expression through AktS473- FoxO1 (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: mTORC2 was found to regulate T-bet expression through AktS473-FoxO1 in NK cells.
source: In NK cells, FoxO1 suppresses NK cell maturation by repressing T-bet (Deng et al., 2015) and mTORC2 was also found to regulate T-bet expression through AktS473- FoxO1 (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: When mTORC2 was knocked out, the expression of T-bet was impaired and Bach2 was upregulated at the mRNA level as a target of FoxO1.
source: When mTORC2 was knocked out, the expression of T-bet was impaired. However, Bach2 was upregulated at the mRNA level as a target of FoxO1 (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Human NK cells encompass two major subsets, known as CD56dim and CD56bright NK cells.
source: Human NK cells encompass two major subsets, known as CD56dim and CD56bright NK cells.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of human NK cell subsets.

claim: CD62L and CCR7 were shown to be highly expressed by CD56bright NK cells and drove their migration to secondary lymphoid tissues.
source: CD62L (encoded by Sell) and CCR7 were shown to be highly expressed by CD56bright NK cells and drove their migration to secondary lymphoid tissues (Campbell et al., 2001; Frey et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CD56bright NK cells expressed high levels of c-Kit for their homeostatic proliferation.
source: CD56bright NK cells also expressed high levels of c-Kit for their homeostatic proliferation (Matos et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Sell, Ccr7, and Kit genes were all downregulated in Bach2-deficient NK cells in mice.
source: In agreement with this, Sell, Ccr7, and Kit genes were all downregulated in Bach2-deficient NK cells in our data in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: CD56dim NK cells displayed a high density of CX3CR1 for the migration to tissues and higher cytotoxic activity by increased expression of perforin and various granzymes.
source: In contrast, CD56dim NK cells displayed a high density of CX3CR1 for the migration to tissues and higher cytotoxic activity by increased expression of perforin and various granzymes (Campbell et al., 2001), which resembled our Bach2-deficient NK phenotypes in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bach2 has been demonstrated to be highly expressed by CD56bright NK cells and with low expression in CD56dim NK cells.
source: More importantly, Bach2 has been demonstrated to be highly expressed by CD56bright NK cells and with low expression in CD56dim NK cells (Holmes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In murine NK cells, Bach2 shows preferential expression in immature CD27+ subsets compared to mature CD11b+ subsets.
source: In murine NK cells, Bach2 also shows preferential expression in immature CD27+ subsets compared to mature CD11b+ subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Bach2 functions as a checkpoint to restrain NK cell cytotoxicity in mice.
source: Our study shows that, in mice, Bach2 functions as a checkpoint to restrain NK cell cytotoxicity and Bach2 deficiency leads to enhanced NK cell-mediated control of B16 melanoma metastases.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor metastasis assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Bach2 deficiency leads to enhanced NK cell-mediated control of B16 melanoma metastases.
source: Our study shows that, in mice, Bach2 functions as a checkpoint to restrain NK cell cytotoxicity and Bach2 deficiency leads to enhanced NK cell-mediated control of B16 melanoma metastases.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor metastasis assay data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Studies in humans have suggested that Bach2 may play a similar role in human NK cells.
source: Studies in humans have also suggested that Bach2 may play a similar role in human NK cells (Collins et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bach2 may be a novel target for checkpoint inhibition of NK cells for cancer immunotherapy.
source: As a result, our study suggests that Bach2 may be a novel target for checkpoint inhibition of NK cells for cancer immunotherapy.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the findings of the study.
